summary: Proposes a non-standard protocol for reliable communication, usable at the second or third level. It considers errors from garbled, lost or misdelivered messages, and discusses ways to improve throughput. The author does not aim to propose a new standard.

eli5.summary: When mail can get lost or smudged, a way to check each letter arrived and read well. This idea makes the connection sturdier.

questions: how to achieve reliable communication on the arpanet
how did early protocols handle message errors
how do you detect lost messages
how do you recover from transmission errors
subtitle: Reliable message exchange over unreliable channels

tldr.problem: Real network channels introduce errors through garbled messages, lost messages, and misdelivered messages. Applications need techniques to detect these errors and recover.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 203 proposes using checksums and parity bits to detect garbled messages, sequence numbers to detect loss, and retransmission with timeouts to recover. The simplest protocol stops after each message until a reply arrives; higher throughput is possible by keeping multiple messages in flight and retransmitting as needed.
tldr.outcome: The RFC explored techniques for reliable communication that became foundational ideas in TCP and other transport protocols, though it was not itself adopted as a standard.

today: This 1971 proposal did not become an ARPA standard. However, its core ideas—checksums, sequence numbers, timeouts, and variable window sizes—became central to TCP and other reliable transport protocols.

sections.title: Error Detection
sections.content: RFC 203 proposes that reliable communication must handle three types of errors: garbled messages (corrupted by bit flips), lost messages (never arriving), and picked-up messages (arriving when not expected). Garbling is detected by checksums or parity bits added by coding theory. Loss and unexpected arrivals are detected with sequence numbers: each message carries a sequence number, and the receiver can tell if a message is out of order or overdue.
sections.eli5: Use a checksum to catch garbled data, and a number on each message to spot lost or out-of-order ones.

sections.title: Retransmission and Throughput
sections.content: The simplest recovery is stop-and-wait: send a message, wait for a reply (or timeout), then send the next one. If no reply arrives within N time units, retransmit. For higher throughput, allow L messages in flight at once: keep sending until L messages lack replies, then retransmit the oldest unreplied message and all newer ones. The trade-off is that larger L increases throughput but makes error recovery more costly.
sections.eli5: Send one letter, wait for an answer. Or send several letters and keep track of which ones got answers, resending stragglers when time runs out.

sections.title: Starting and Stopping
sections.content: Opening a connection faces a race: both sides need to agree on the first sequence number. The RFC proposes repeating the first message until the same reply is received K times (for example, 50 times). Once received, sequencing is adjusted and normal messages begin. Closing is equally tricky: a host sends messages until it gets a reply to the last one, then stops. If no reply arrives within J seconds, it ceases retransmission. To avoid confusion between a broken channel and the end of conversation, J should be less than N times K.
sections.eli5: To start, send the first letter many times until you hear back the same reply many times. To stop, send your last letter, get an answer, and then wait to see if anything else comes before you say goodbye.
